finding.claim: Unauthenticated POST /restore passes attacker-supplied base64 to Marshal.load, a code-execution-class deserialization sink. Gadget availability depends on production gems, which were not visible.
finding.source: params[:state] from any POST to /restore (query or body), no auth required
finding.sink: Marshal.load(Base64.decode64(params[:state])) at app.rb:6; state.inspect returned at app.rb:7

trace.note: post "/restore" is a public route with no before filter or auth check
params[:state] passed to Base64.decode64, which never rejects malformed input
decoded bytes passed to Marshal.load with no class allowlist

finding.guards_checked: None in this file: no auth, no type or schema validation, no size limit, no HMAC or signature on state, no safe alternative to Marshal. Sinatra default Rack::Protection does not stop a direct non-browser POST.

verdict.guard_found: none. app.rb:5 is a public `post "/restore"` route with no before filter or auth. app.rb:6 calls `Marshal.load(Base64.decode64(params[:state]))` with no class allowlist, size limit, signature, or safe alternative. app.rb:7 returns `state.inspect` to the caller. The file has no other controls, and the Glob shows no other source files.
verdict.reason: The attacker is anonymous and reaches the unauthenticated POST route at app.rb:5, where attacker-controlled `params[:state]` is base64-decoded and passed straight to `Marshal.load` at app.rb:6 with no effective guard, so the deserialization sink is reachable. Whether it yields code execution depends on gadgets in the production gem set, which this file does not show, but Marshal.load on untrusted input is a code-execution-class sink regardless, so the finding stands as a high-severity vulnerability.

finding.claim: /import reflects attacker-controlled JSON key names into the response body, which Sinatra serves as text/html by default. Likely mitigated by default Rack::Protection HttpOrigin for cross-site attacks, but not verified against an installed Sinatra.
finding.source: Raw request body parsed as JSON at app.rb:11; every key name is attacker-controlled
finding.sink: data.keys.join(",") returned as response body at app.rb:12, rendered as text/html

trace.note: keys joined and returned unescaped with default text/html content type

finding.guards_checked: POST-only route, so GET cannot trigger it. Cross-site form needs a text/plain body that parses as JSON. Sinatra default Rack::Protection HttpOrigin should reject a mismatched Origin, unverified here. No HTML escaping and no explicit Content-Type in this file.

verdict.guard_found: None in app.rb: no authentication, no HTML escaping, no explicit Content-Type (app.rb:10-12). The only candidate control is Sinatra's default Rack::Protection HttpOrigin middleware, which is not in this directory (the only file is app.rb, with no Gemfile or Gemfile.lock to confirm the Sinatra version or protection settings).
verdict.reason: The trace matches app.rb:10-12 (a POST route parses the raw body as JSON and returns the attacker-chosen key names as an unescaped text/html response), and an anonymous attacker can reach it, but whether a cross-site browser attack works depends on Sinatra's default HttpOrigin protection, which is library code not present here, so the finding can't be settled from the code available.

finding.claim: Unhandled exceptions expose stack traces to clients. Sinatra defaults to development when RACK_ENV and APP_ENV are unset, which enables show_exceptions. Malformed /restore input and a non-object /import body such as [1] (NoMethodError at line 12) both trigger this.
finding.source: Malformed or wrong-shape request body to /restore or /import
finding.sink: Uncaught exception rendered as a backtrace response (Marshal error at app.rb:6, NoMethodError at app.rb:12)

trace.note: Marshal.load raises on malformed bytes, no rescue
data.keys raises NoMethodError when data is an Array or scalar, no rescue

finding.guards_checked: No rescue blocks, no set :show_exceptions false, no environment pinning in this file. Depends on deployment environment, not verified.

verdict.guard_found: none in app.rb: no rescue blocks, no `set :show_exceptions false`, no environment pinning. The repo has only app.rb, so no config.ru or Gemfile pins RACK_ENV/APP_ENV. Sinatra's default environment is development when both are unset, and its default show_exceptions is development-only, which is the framework default rather than code in this repo.
verdict.reason: app.rb:6 (Marshal.load on params[:state]) and app.rb:12 (data.keys on the JSON.parse result at line 11) have no rescue, and an anonymous client can send malformed input to either route, so with Sinatra's default development environment the uncaught exception is rendered with a backtrace. The result depends on deployment not setting RACK_ENV or APP_ENV to production, which this repo cannot show, so severity is low, and the same line 6 Marshal.load is a far more serious deserialization issue than this finding.

finding.claim: No input size limits on /import body or /restore state. Large or deeply nested payloads cause resource exhaustion (DoS), not code execution.
finding.source: Unbounded request body at app.rb:11 and unbounded params[:state] at app.rb:6
finding.sink: JSON.parse and Marshal.load allocate memory proportional to payload size and nesting

trace.note: request.body.read reads the full body with no cap
params[:state] decoded and deserialized with no cap

finding.guards_checked: None in this file. Server or proxy limits may exist outside the repo, not checked.

verdict.guard_found: none in the repo. app.rb:11 reads the full body with request.body.read and no size cap, and app.rb:6 passes params[:state] straight into Base64.decode64 and Marshal.load with no length or depth check. Both routes are unauthenticated (no auth filter or before-block in app.rb). Any web server or proxy limit sits outside the repo and was not checked.
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate: app.rb:11 reads the whole request body into JSON.parse with no cap, and app.rb:6 deserializes an unbounded params[:state] via Marshal.load, both on unauthenticated routes, so an anonymous client can force large allocations. Verdict holds for the resource-exhaustion claim only; note that Marshal.load on attacker-controlled input at app.rb:6 is a far more serious issue (deserialization gadget/code execution risk) than the candidate's "not code execution" framing suggests.
